question: You're building a pipeline that uses LLMs to interpret LIDAR point clouds for urban planning. Walk me through your decision matrix: local Ollama deployment vs. cloud APIs vs. fine-tuned open models. What specific performance metrics drive your choice?

maya.content: For community-controlled urban planning, local Ollama deployment is non-negotiable—our data sovereignty requirements prohibit cloud processing of territorial information. We measure success by community trust metrics alongside technical performance; 200ms inference latency is acceptable if it means local control. Our decision matrix prioritizes data residency compliance, then model accuracy on indigenous place names and traditional land use categories, with throughput as a secondary concern since community consultation processes aren't time-critical.

otto.content: The decision hinges on point cloud density and processing requirements—for high-resolution urban LIDAR (>10 points/m²), we need models that understand 3D spatial relationships accurately. Local Ollama with Llama 70B provides better geometric reasoning than cloud APIs, but requires 80GB VRAM minimum. I evaluate models using spatial accuracy metrics: building footprint precision, elevation model RMSE, and topology preservation scores. Fine-tuned models trained on annotated point cloud datasets consistently outperform general-purpose LLMs by 15-20% on urban feature classification tasks.

sarah.content: Open model fine-tuning offers the best long-term value for community-driven urban planning—we can adapt models to local building codes and zoning requirements without vendor lock-in. Our benchmark suite measures inference cost per point cloud tile, model accuracy on building height estimation, and integration compatibility with existing FOSS tools like PDAL and CloudCompare. Local deployment wins for privacy and customization, but cloud APIs provide better scalability for regional planning initiatives. We typically start local for prototyping, then evaluate cloud migration based on processing volume.

marcus.content: Production urban planning requires sub-100ms inference latency for interactive applications, which drives us toward optimized cloud deployments with edge caching. Our decision matrix weighs processing throughput (points per second), accuracy on infrastructure detection, and total cost of ownership including GPU infrastructure. Fine-tuned models provide 25% better accuracy on urban feature extraction, but local Ollama deployment limits scalability to single-city projects. We use hybrid architectures: sensitive preliminary planning on local models, final analysis on cloud infrastructure with appropriate data handling agreements.

jessica.content: Mission-critical urban infrastructure analysis demands air-gapped local deployment—cloud APIs introduce unacceptable security risks for critical facility planning. We measure model performance using defense-specific metrics: accuracy on identifying potential security vulnerabilities, precision in infrastructure asset classification, and reliability under adversarial inputs. Our deployment uses hardened Ollama instances with custom model weights optimized for infrastructure analysis. Processing latency is less critical than accuracy and security; we accept 500ms inference times to maintain complete data control and model auditability.
